claims.text: A controlled post-synthesis low-temperature oxidation treatment can form an in situ high-entropy oxide overlayer on the starting alloy catalyst.
The oxide-forming treatment can simultaneously enhance catalytic activity and durability under transient low-temperature exhaust conditions.
The starting material is a nearly equiatomic multi-element alloy catalyst with low platinum-group-metal content.
The treatment should anneal the catalyst at approximately 300°C in oxygen containing minor NO and water vapor.
Treatment at approximately 300°C can form an ultrathin conformal oxide without causing excessive diffusion or sintering.
The resulting overlayer will be a spinel- or perovskite-like high-entropy oxide.
The overlayer will be enriched in stable non-PGM metal oxides.
Mild oxidation triggers selective oxidation and surface reconstruction of the alloy.
The oxide overlayer protects the catalyst by limiting sintering and elemental dissolution.
The oxide overlayer passivates active sites.
The oxide overlayer optimizes oxygen-vacancy populations.
Optimized oxygen vacancies improve adsorption and desorption of NO, water, and other exhaust intermediates.
Improved adsorption and desorption increases catalytic turnover.
Compared with the untreated catalyst, the treated catalyst will retain greater activity and have lower activation barriers for critical exhaust-conversion steps.
Compared with the untreated catalyst, the treated catalyst will have enhanced durability during thermal aging and exposure to H2O and NO.
The untreated automotive alloy catalyst typically loses activity and durability under transient low-temperature operation and thermal aging.
The proposed benefit depends on the oxide remaining ultrathin and conformal at exhaust operating temperatures.
Conditions substantially more severe than the treatment conditions may reduce the overlayer's effectiveness.
Excessive oxide growth can impede gas transport and catalytic performance.
